function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I don’t have the ability to run shell commands, clone repositories, or push commits from here.  
What I can do is give you a concrete plan and the exact files you’ll need to add to the **nodejs‑welcome** repo so that you can finish the task locally (or in your CI environment).

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re doing this inside a CI job, just `git clone` the repo into the workspace.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a typical Node.js app (`app.js` or `index.js`) and a `package.json`, a minimal Dockerfile would look like:

```Dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
RUN npm run build || true   # optional – only if you have a build script

FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

If you prefer to use the helper function:

```python
# In a small script or notebook
import functions

functions.create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name=".",          # current repo root
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,
    entrypoint='["npm","start"]'
)
```

> The function will write a `Dockerfile` in the given directory.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

A simple deployment + service for a Node.js app listening on port 3000:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

Using the helper:

```python
functions.create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name="k8s",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome",
    image_name="zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=3,
    port=3000,
    service_type="LoadBalancer"
)
```

> The function will create a `k8s/deployment.yaml` (and a `k8s/service.yaml` if you want separate files).

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }},zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> Make sure you store your Docker Hub credentials in the repo’s *Settings → Secrets* as `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

If you used the helper functions, they already wrote the files; just stage them.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically build and push a Docker image whenever you push to `main`. The Kubernetes manifests can be applied with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image tags, or service type to fit your environment. Happy coding!
